name: Americares: medicine donations and health services (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result by branch at the defaults (clinics 41%, medicine donations to clinics 29%, health-worker training 28%, the US patient-assistance programme 1%); clinics split equally over Colombia, El Salvador, India and the US, donations 20% US (restricted gifts' split, statements note 7) and the rest, with the training, equally over the seven programme countries named in the annual report (Colombia, El Salvador, India, Haiti, Liberia, Malawi, the Philippines): a judgment, as Americares publishes no country split.
summary: Americares, a US health and disaster-relief charity, ships donated medicines and supplies (1.73 billion dollars at recorded US wholesale value in its fiscal year to June 2025) to partner clinics and hospitals in the US and abroad and to US patients through drug companies' patient-assistance programmes, and runs its own clinics in Colombia, El Salvador, India and Connecticut and community health projects in 36 countries. This model covers those two programmes' 93 million dollars of cash spending in four branches: the patient-assistance programme, medicine donations to clinics (1.9 million patients by Americares' estimate), its clinics (364,468 consultations) and health-worker training, each as deaths and illness averted; donated medicines and partners' own costs count in the credit share, not the cost. The result is about {{result}} years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars because the donated medicine, valued at what it costs where it's used, and the partners' staff are nearly all of the resources behind the donations, so Americares' cash is credited with under a tenth of their effect, and drug companies would most likely run their assistance programmes without it. Every branch's effect is our judgment (no study measures what donated medicine or these clinics do), so all four are discounted by the shared missing-data slider, and the result is mostly uncertainty. Emergency programmes are a separate model.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

story.sentence: $1,000 sends donated medicines and runs clinics, reaching **{1000 * people_reached / cost_total} patients** in the US and abroad.

rows.label: Recorded value of one patient's medicine for a year
rows.explainer: Brand-name medicines for chronic illness (diabetes, asthma and COPD inhalers, heart disease, HIV, some cancer drugs) list at about 250 to 1,000 dollars a month in the US; a patient enrolled for part of the year gets less. Our judgment, 6,000 dollars a patient-year, from 3,000 (mostly cheaper brands) to 15,000 (specialty drugs). It turns the donated value into patients and carries the branch's reach, which Americares doesn't publish.

rows.explainer: Visits, not people: divided by visits per patient below.

rows.label: Consultations per patient in a year at Americares' clinics
rows.explainer: Primary-care clinics see most patients a few times a year; the chronic-disease patients of the Connecticut clinics and El Salvador's poverty programme more often, the India mobile units' walk-ins less. Our judgment, 2.5, from 1.5 to 4.

rows.label: Patients at Americares-run clinics
rows.explainer: About 146,000 patients.

rows.explainer: Health workers at partner health centres trained by Americares' community health projects (infectious disease, mental health, maternal and child health, water and sanitation, climate resilience) in the year.

rows.label: Patients reached in the year (all branches)
rows.explainer: Patient-years of assistance-programme medicine, patients helped by donated medicine and clinic patients; the training projects reach patients through the health workers, counted in their own rows.

rows.label: Cost per patient reached
rows.explainer: Context only: the full cost of the two programmes over the patients.

rows.label: Years of care per patient counted
rows.explainer: The risks below are per patient-year of medicine (assistance programme) or per patient over the year's care (clinics, donations), so one year; the low end, half a year, for patients who get a single course. Based on the clinics' 2.5 consultations per patient a year (hs_visits_per_patient), most patients are in care through the year. Used for the wait to the middle of the benefit.

rows.label: Assistance-programme patients: yearly risk of death
rows.explainer: Uninsured, low-income US adults on medicine for chronic illness (diabetes, heart and lung disease, HIV, some cancers); US adults 45-64 die at about 0.7% a year (CDC WONDER) and these patients are sicker and older than average. Our judgment, 1.5% a year, from 0.8% to 3%.

rows.label: Assistance-programme patients: share of that risk the medicine removes
rows.explainer: For a patient who would otherwise go without (whether they would is the counterfactual below): statins and blood-pressure drugs cut deaths by 10-20% in trials, insulin and HIV drugs by far more, inhalers and many brand drugs very little against a cheaper generic the patient could buy. Our judgment, 12% of the risk, from 5% to 25%.

rows.label: Assistance-programme deaths averted: share aged 15-49 (rest 50-74)
rows.explainer: The patients are uninsured adults under 65 (Medicare covers most people from 65) with chronic disease, mostly cardiovascular and metabolic: the shared rich-country split of cardiovascular deaths between 15-49 and 50-69 (WHO Global Health Estimates, the UK's, the nearest the site holds to the US) gives about {{row:pap_share_15_49}} under 50, the rest at the 50-74 weight.

rows.label: Assistance-programme: value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's one value of a death by age band, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Assistance-programme: illness averted per patient-year (DALYs)
rows.explainer: Symptoms controlled for a year (breathlessness, high blood sugar, angina, pain) against going without: a disability-weight gain of 0.01 to 0.05 for a year (GBD 2019 weights for moderate COPD, diabetes complications or heart failure are 0.02-0.2) for part of the patients. Our judgment, 0.01 DALY a patient-year, from 0.003 to 0.03.

rows.label: Assistance-programme medicines: what they cost in the market, as a share of their recorded (list) value
rows.explainer: Donated goods count at what they would cost on the market where they're used, not list prices (families/humanitarian-relief.md). US brand-drug net prices after rebates are about half of list on average (IQVIA and SSR Health estimates of 40-60% discounts on brand medicines); the uninsured would pay closer to list. Our judgment, 50%, from 30% to 80%.

rows.label: Assistance-programme: share of the medicine patients wouldn't have got anyway
rows.explainer: Americares administers drug companies' own assistance programmes: without it, the companies would most likely run them in-house or through another administrator (most large companies run their own patient-assistance foundations), and some patients would get the drug through Medicaid or another programme. What Americares adds is mainly patients reached through its clinic network who wouldn't find another programme. Our judgment, 15%, from 5% to 40%.

rows.label: Assistance-programme: Americares' share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: Americares' cash cost against the companies' medicines at market value (Convention 2: donated goods are the donors' resources). About 2%: the medicine is nearly all the resource.

rows.label: Assistance-programme: counted less for missing outcome data
rows.explainer: Thin: no count of patients (reach is the donated value over a judged price per patient-year) and no study of what the medicine does for these patients against going without.

rows.label: Patients given donated medicine: risk of death without treatment
rows.explainer: Patients at partner clinics and hospitals (mostly outpatients: infections, high blood pressure, diabetes, pain, wound care) in low- and middle-income countries and US safety-net clinics. As MSF's outpatient branch in our model of its medical care (0.2%, from 0.07% to 0.5%), for a mix with fewer young children and fewer emergencies.

rows.label: Patients given donated medicine: share of that risk treatment removes
rows.explainer: As MSF's outpatient branch (30%, from 15% to 50%): antibiotics, antimalarials and chronic-disease drugs remove much of the risk when needed, much of the medicine treats conditions that seldom kill.

rows.label: Donated-medicine deaths averted: share under five
rows.explainer: Partner facilities treat all ages; young children die most of infections in poor countries, while US clinics and chronic-disease drugs serve adults. Anchors from the shared splits: under-fives are 55% of diarrhoea and 63% of malaria deaths in sub-Saharan Africa but 0.2% of cardiovascular deaths worldwide (@death_ages); the donated medicine treats both kinds. Our judgment, 20%, from 10% to 40%.

rows.label: Donated-medicine deaths averted at five or older: share aged 5-14
rows.explainer: Older children have the lowest death rates of any age: about 10% of deaths over five, as in our relief models.

rows.label: Donated-medicine deaths averted at 15 or older: share aged 15-49
rows.explainer: Adult deaths from treatable conditions in low- and middle-income countries fall between working ages and 50-plus: 15-49 are 37% of adult diarrhoea and 68% of adult HIV deaths in sub-Saharan Africa but 7% of cardiovascular deaths worldwide (@death_ages shares). Our judgment for the mix, 40%, from 25% to 55%; the rest at the 50-74 weight.

rows.label: Donated medicine: value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's one value of a death by age band, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Donated medicine: illness averted per patient (DALYs)
rows.explainer: An infection cured a week or two sooner (GBD weight for moderate acute infection 0.051 × two weeks = 0.002) or a chronic condition controlled for months (0.01-0.03). Our judgment, 0.005 DALY a patient, from 0.002 to 0.015.

rows.label: Donated medicines and supplies to clinics and hospitals (recorded value)
rows.explainer: The medicine programme's donated goods other than the assistance programme's, about 384 million dollars at recorded value.

rows.label: Donated medicines: market price where used, as a share of recorded value
rows.explainer: Medicines abroad are recorded at US wholesale prices where sold in the US (p. 13), while partner countries buy generics at a fraction (international reference prices are often a tenth to a fifth of US list prices); US safety-net clinics would pay near US prices. Restricted gifts went 80% abroad (189.7 vs 47.5 million dollars, p. 19). Our judgment, 30%, from 10% to 60%.

rows.label: Partner facilities' own costs of the care, as a multiple of the medicine's market value
rows.explainer: The medicines reach patients through partner clinics' and hospitals' staff, buildings and diagnosis, paid by governments, other donors and patients. Reference class: WHO-CHOICE outpatient costs, in which medicines are a third to a half of the cost of a visit in low-income primary care, so the facility's other costs are one to two times the medicine; in US free clinics volunteers' time is worth more, while hospitals given surgical supplies or chronic-disease drugs add less. Our judgment, as much again as the medicine, from half to twice.

rows.label: Donated medicine: Americares' share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: Americares' cash against the companies' medicines at market value and the partner facilities' own costs (Convention 2). About 8%.

rows.label: Donated medicine: share of patients who wouldn't have been treated anyway
rows.explainer: Partner facilities in poor countries often run out of essential medicines (median availability of generics in public facilities about 40-60%, WHO/HAI surveys) and their patients can't always buy them; but some patients would buy the drug or get it elsewhere, and some donations replace stock the facility would have bought. Our judgment, 40%, from 20% to 70%.

rows.label: Donated medicine: share used as intended before it expires
rows.explainer: Americares holds a 30 million dollar allowance for expiring or damaged stock against 317 million of inventory (p. 18) and reports destruction among other expenses; donated medicines are often near expiry. Our judgment, 85% used, from 70% to 95%.

rows.label: Donated medicine: counted less for missing outcome data
rows.explainer: Thin: the patients are Americares' estimate and no study measures what donated medicine does for patients against a stock-out.

rows.label: Share of the health-services spending that runs Americares' own clinics
rows.explainer: The programme runs four Connecticut free clinics, a clinic in El Salvador, 12 mobile units in Mumbai and clinics for Venezuelan migrants in Colombia (the 2.2 million dollar State Department award, p. 28, is one), and 270 community projects in 36 countries. Its 15.7 million dollars of salaries and 10.6 million of professional fees (p. 8) point to clinics, its 25.9 million of other grants and relief supplies to projects. Our judgment, half each. Context: it splits the cost between clinics and projects for the reading-only averages; the result is the two together over their joint cost.

rows.label: Americares-run clinics: cash spending
Community health projects: cash spending
Clinic patients: risk of death in the year without the clinic's care
rows.explainer: Primary care for low-income adults and families (chronic disease, infections, antenatal care) in middle-income Colombia, El Salvador and India and in the US. Reference class: deaths amenable to health care (causes timely care can avert, such as hypertension, diabetes and treatable cancers) were 109 a year per 100,000 people under 75 in the US in 2002-03, about 0.1% (Nolte and McKee 2008, Health Affairs 27: 58-71). The clinics' patients are poorer and sicker than average (they come because they are ill), and amenable mortality is higher in the three middle-income countries: twice that, 0.2%, from 0.07% to 0.5%.

rows.label: Clinic patients: share of that risk the care removes
rows.explainer: Diagnosis and treatment of chronic and acute illness, few of them deadly acute infections; a judgment with no reference class.

rows.label: Clinic deaths averted: share under five
rows.explainer: The clinics mostly serve adults with chronic disease; the India and Colombia clinics see children too. Between the shared splits for cardiovascular deaths (0.2% under five) and infections (over half, @death_ages). Our judgment, 15%, from 5% to 30%.

rows.label: Clinics: value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's one value of a death by age band (older ages as the donated-medicine patients), times your value of a life.

rows.label: Clinic patients: illness averted per patient (DALYs)
rows.explainer: Chronic disease controlled, infections treated, depression and anxiety counselled (9,227 mental-health consultations, p. 12): a disability-weight gain of 0.02-0.05 for a few months. Our judgment, 0.01 DALY a patient.

rows.label: Clinic patients: share who wouldn't have got this care anyway
rows.explainer: Colombia's and El Salvador's public systems and Mumbai's municipal clinics exist but are hard to reach for migrants, the rural poor and slum residents; US uninsured patients have community health centres. Our judgment, half, from 30% to 70%.

rows.label: Clinics: Americares' share of the resources behind the care
rows.explainer: Americares employs the staff and pays for the clinics; volunteers (the Connecticut clinics' volunteer doctors) and donated medicines (5.9 million dollars recorded, p. 8) are others' resources. Our judgment, 85%.

rows.label: Clinics: counted less for missing outcome data
rows.explainer: Thin: consultations are counted, but what the care does for these patients is our judgment, not measured.

rows.label: Patients a trained health worker sees in a year
rows.explainer: Community health workers see a few hundred people a year, clinic nurses and doctors several thousand; the trainees are a mix. Our judgment, 500, from 200 to 1,500.

rows.label: Illness and deaths averted per patient seen by a trained worker (DALYs)
rows.explainer: Training alone raises health workers' adherence to guidelines by about 10 percentage points on average (Rowe et al. 2018, Lancet Global Health systematic review, https://doi.org/10.1016/S2214-109X(18)30398-X); against 0.01-0.03 DALYs at stake in a typical primary-care patient's illness, a few hundredths of that is averted. Our judgment, 0.0002 DALY a patient, from 0.00005 to 0.001; deaths are in this figure.

rows.label: Years a training's effect lasts
rows.explainer: Training effects fade without supervision and staff move on (Rowe et al. 2018 find smaller effects at longer follow-up). Our judgment, two years.

rows.label: Community projects: DALYs averted before adjustments
rows.explainer: Trained workers × their patients × the gain per patient over the years it lasts, discounted. The projects' water, mental-health and climate-resilience work is valued through the same trained workers and the unmodelled share. Some trainees work in partner clinics that also get donated medicine; the gain here is better care, a different effect from the medicine, so the overlap (at most a few percent of the result) is accepted.

rows.label: Community projects: share that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Some of the training would have come from ministries or other NGOs; the 2025 cuts to US foreign aid left more gaps than usual. Our judgment, 70%.

rows.label: Community projects: Americares' share of the resources
rows.explainer: Partners' and ministries' staff time in training and the health centres' own costs are others' resources. Our judgment, 60%.

rows.label: Community projects: counted less for missing outcome data
rows.explainer: Thin: built from the research on training health workers, with no outcome data from these projects.

rows.label: Risk of death without the care (patient-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (pap_people * pap_risk_untreated + don_people * don_risk_untreated + hs_people * hs_risk_untreated) / people_reached
rows.explainer: Each branch's risk per patient-year or patient, weighted by its patients.

rows.label: Share of the risk removed (risk-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (pap_people * pap_risk_untreated * pap_risk_reduction + don_people * don_risk_untreated * don_risk_reduction + hs_people * hs_risk_untreated * hs_risk_reduction) / (pap_people * pap_risk_untreated + don_people * don_risk_untreated + hs_people * hs_risk_untreated)
rows.explainer: Each branch's reduction weighted by its deaths at risk.

rows.label: Indirect deaths averted per direct death
rows.explainer: 0: the risks above are all-cause deaths of the patients treated, so no indirect deaths are added.

rows.label: Deaths averted per patient (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Deaths averted before adjustments over all patients; the branches' risks are already per patient-year or per patient, so no years multiply them.

rows.label: Share of deaths averted under five (for reading only)
rows.formula: (don_people * don_risk_untreated * don_risk_reduction * don_share_under5 + hs_people * hs_risk_untreated * hs_risk_reduction * hs_share_under5) / (pap_people * pap_risk_untreated * pap_risk_reduction + don_people * don_risk_untreated * don_risk_reduction + hs_people * hs_risk_untreated * hs_risk_reduction)
rows.explainer: The branches' under-five shares weighted by their deaths averted (assistance-programme patients are adults).

rows.label: Of deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5-14 (for reading)
rows.explainer: As the donated-medicine and clinic branches.

rows.label: Of deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15-49 (for reading)
rows.explainer: As the donated-medicine and clinic branches; the assistance programme has its own split.

rows.label: Illness as a share of the deaths' value
rows.explainer: 0: illness is counted in DALYs, branch by branch (the *_dalys_illness rows), so it isn't added again as a share.

rows.label: Stillbirths averted per patient
rows.explainer: 0: antenatal care at the clinics is a small part of the work; any stillbirths averted are in the illness and deaths figures' ranges.

rows.label: Later-life income gain (ln consumption a year)
rows.explainer: 0: no evidence that the care changes later income; healthier adults working more is in the unmodelled share.

rows.label: Years until the income gain
rows.explainer: No income gain is counted, so no wait.

rows.label: Years the income gain lasts
rows.explainer: The site's one figure (unused at a gain of 0).

rows.label: Income gain per patient (discounted ln consumption)
Household sharing of income gains
rows.explainer: The site's one figure (unused at a gain of 0).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment: how far the judged effects hold for these patients
rows.explainer: Every effect above is a judgment anchored on outpatient care elsewhere (MSF's), not a trial of donated medicine or these clinics: some donated drugs treat conditions that seldom kill, quality of care at partner facilities varies. Our judgment, 0.8, from 0.6 to 1.

rows.label: Internal validity of the evidence
rows.explainer: 1: there is no trial to discount; the doubt about the judged effects is in the external-validity row.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: The product of its two parts.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Americares takes little government money (3.1 million dollars, 2% of cash revenue), so a donation neither displaces nor pulls in much public money; others filling in is in each branch's counterfactual. 1, with a small range.

rows.label: Cash and investments at year end

source.title: Americares Foundation, Inc. and Affiliate: consolidated financial statements, years ended June 30, 2025 and 2024 (Grant Thornton, audited)

rows.explainer: Money held at 30 June 2025 (11.663 + 43.295 million dollars), for the wait between a gift and its use.

rows.label: Years a gift waits before it's spent
rows.explainer: Money held over a year's cash spending: about {{row:gift_to_grant_years}} years.

rows.label: Years from spending to the patient's treatment
rows.explainer: Donated medicine sits in Americares' and partners' stores for months before it's dispensed (inventory of 317 million dollars against 1.75 billion distributed a year: about two months, p. 18), and clinic care is immediate. Our judgment, 0.3 years.

rows.label: Years to the middle of the benefit
Discount for the wait
rows.explainer: The waits together, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Assistance programme: all adjustments combined
rows.formula: evidence_adj * pap_counterfactual_adj * pap_attribution_share * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount * pap_missing_data_adj

rows.label: Other benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Benefits: supply-chain and disaster-preparedness support to partner clinics (the climate-resilience toolkits, pre-positioned stock), healthier adults working more, water and sanitation in the projects (+). Harms: donated near-expiry medicine that partners must destroy, donations displacing local purchases, and assistance programmes steering patients to brand drugs and earning companies tax deductions (−). Our judgment, +5%, from −15% to +20%.
